To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
neurospheres can be isolated from the adult spinal cord and subependymal forebrain of adult mice after protracted postmortem intervals.
neurospheres can be generated after long postmortem intervals from the spinal cord and subependymal zones of the forebrain of adult mice.
neurosphere-generat- ing cells can be obtained from adult mouse spinal cords and forebrain sub-ependymal zone even after prolonged postmortem intervals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation and characterization of neural stem/progenitor cell lines from adult mouse brain and spinal cord, and with their use in the generation of transplantable cells for CNS repair.
the isolation and characterization of multipotent stem cells from adult spinal cord and fore brain subependymal zones after prolonged postmortem intervals.

the ability of neurospheres to be generated from the adult CNS under postmortem conditions, which is of importance for the study of the neurogenic potential of the adult CNS and for the development of stem cell-based therapies for neurologic disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
postmortem neurosphere cultures can be used to isolate and study adult stem/progenitor cell populations.

neurosphere-forming cells are present in adult mammalian brain and spinal cord after postmortem periods up to at least 30 h at room temperature and 140 h at 4 degreesC, and that these cells retain the ability to proliferate and differentiate into neurons and glia in vitro.

neurosphere-generators can be isolated from the adult mouse spinal cord, and the adult mouse forebrain subependymanl zone up to 140 hours postmortem when stored at 4 degrees celsius, and up to thirty hours postmortem if stored at room temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

neurosphere-generators can be obtained from the CNS of adult mice after postmortem periods that are compatible with the time required to transport tissue from a remote location, and that the resulting neurospheres are capable of generating neurons and glia.
the neurospheres generated from adult mouse spinal cords and forebrains after protracted postmortem intervals are multipotent and are therefore likely to be derived from stem cells.
, in the CNS, multipotent stem cells exist not only in vivo but also in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neurosphere-generat- ing cells are remarkably robust to postmortem intervals and can be isolated and cultured from both spinal cord and fore-brain subependymal zones.
the postmortem time window is a crucial factor that should be taken into consideration for the isolation of neurosphere-forming cells from adult CNS tissues.
postmortem tissue can be used to generate neurospheres, which could be a useful source of material to study CNS stem cells and neurogenesis.
